paragraphs: Diffusion generators rely on a sequence of numerical updates to produce samples. This paper studies how the choice of those updates affects convergence, using Wasserstein distance to measure the difference between the generated and desired distributions. Its focus is the mathematical behavior of sampling procedures, including how accurately their discrete steps approximate the underlying process.

The authors quantitatively compare Euler discretization, exponential integrators, and midpoint randomization. They also investigate a setting where Hessian information is available, providing information about local curvature. For that setting, they introduce an accelerated sampler based on local linearization and establish a Wasserstein convergence analysis for it.

The resulting rate improves from the standard order of d divided by epsilon squared to the square root of d divided by epsilon, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here, d represents dimension and epsilon the accuracy target. This improvement belongs to the analyzed Hessian-based setting. Experiments on synthetic data and MNIST support the theoretical findings, connecting the analysis to observed sampling behavior.
neurips-2025-advancing-wasserstein-conve.tldr: The paper compares diffusion sampling discretizations and establishes a faster Wasserstein convergence rate for a sampler that uses Hessian information.

paragraphs: Web agents often need personal information to complete tasks, but access alone does not make every use appropriate. AgentDAM evaluates data minimization: whether an agent uses potentially sensitive information only when it is necessary for its assigned task. This makes privacy a question about the agent's actual behavior throughout a workflow.

The benchmark simulates realistic web interactions from beginning to end and is designed to accommodate existing web-navigation agents. The authors evaluate agents built on GPT-4, Llama-3, and Claude. Their findings show that these agents are prone to inadvertently using sensitive information that the task does not require.

The paper also introduces a prompting-based defense that reduces leakage. Its end-to-end evaluation provides a more realistic measure of privacy behavior than asking a language model privacy questions in isolation. Together, these results show why an agent's expressed understanding of privacy needs to be checked against its actions. The defense improves behavior, while the findings still motivate further work on data minimization during inference.
neurips-2025-agentdam-privacy-leakage-ev.tldr: AgentDAM tests whether web agents use only necessary personal information and finds inadvertent leakage that a prompting defense reduces.

paragraphs: Language models keep a key-value cache of information from earlier tokens to support generation. Compressing that cache requires identifying which entries will remain useful. The paper argues that methods based on static attention scores miss how attention changes over time, which can cause them to discard important information and reduce model performance.

AttentionPredictor learns to forecast attention scores for the next token. A lightweight convolutional model captures patterns across tokens and time, and the same prediction model is shared across transformer layers with negligible memory consumption. This turns cache selection into a prediction problem informed by the evolving attention history.

The system also prefetches critical cache entries across tokens, hiding the time spent estimating their importance to accelerate decoding. In a cache offloading scenario, the authors report 13-fold cache compression and a 5.6-fold speedup with comparable language-model performance. These results show the benefit of combining predictive token selection with a retrieval schedule that reduces its overhead; the reported speedup specifically concerns the offloading setting.
neurips-2025-attentionpredictor-temporal.tldr: AttentionPredictor forecasts changing attention patterns to compress the KV cache, reporting 13-fold compression and a 5.6-fold speedup in an offloading scenario.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from past experience becomes difficult when the recorded data contain hidden sources of bias. This paper studies off-policy reinforcement learning in complex, high-dimensional environments where unobserved confounding cannot be ruled out. The concern is that the observations may support misleading conclusions about which actions produce good outcomes.

The authors build on the Deep Q-Network approach and introduce an algorithm intended to withstand confounding in the available experience. It attempts to find a safe policy for the worst-case environment compatible with the observations. This explicitly incorporates uncertainty about the environment that generated the data into policy learning.

The method is evaluated on twelve Atari games with confounding. The authors report that it consistently outperforms standard DQN in all games where the behavioral and target policies receive mismatched observed inputs and unobserved confounders exist. That qualification matters: the stated empirical advantage concerns these confounded, mismatched-input settings. The contribution connects causal concerns about biased experience with a practical deep reinforcement-learning algorithm.
neurips-2025-confounding-robust-deep-rei.tldr: A DQN-based method seeks policies robust to hidden confounding and outperforms standard DQN in the reported confounded, mismatched-input Atari settings.

paragraphs: A time series can reveal different patterns when viewed at fine and coarse sampling scales. CrossAD addresses the possibility that an anomaly changes the relationship between those views. Existing approaches often process scales separately or combine their features simply, leaving these changing relationships insufficiently modeled.

The framework reconstructs fine-grained series from coarser versions. This makes the relationship between scales an explicit modeling target, rather than only collecting information from each scale. CrossAD also introduces a query library and incorporates global context across multiple scales to address the restricted context available inside a fixed sliding window.

These components address two connected gaps: how different resolutions relate to one another and how much surrounding information the detector can use. The authors evaluate CrossAD on seven real-world datasets with nine evaluation metrics and report state-of-the-art anomaly detection performance. The findings support modeling cross-scale associations and context beyond fixed windows together when searching for anomalous temporal behavior.
neurips-2025-crossad-time-series-anomaly.tldr: CrossAD improves time-series anomaly detection by learning relationships between sampling scales and incorporating context beyond fixed windows.

paragraphs: DeepVideo-R1 investigates reinforcement-learning post-training for video language models. It focuses on Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, which uses rewards normalized within groups. The authors identify two obstacles to effective learning in this setting: dependence on optimization safeguards and vanishing advantages, which weaken the signals used to guide improvement.

Their Reg-GRPO method turns the loss into a regression task that directly predicts the GRPO advantage. This removes the need for safeguards such as clipping and minimum operations in that formulation. By aligning the model directly with advantages, the objective supplies guidance toward better outcomes.

A second component changes prompts or videos according to sample difficulty, aiming to place examples at difficulty levels the model can solve. This encourages diverse reward signals and complements the revised objective. Experiments show significant improvements in video reasoning across multiple benchmarks. The overall approach addresses both how feedback is translated into a training objective and whether the training examples produce useful feedback in the first place.
neurips-2025-deepvideo-r1-video-reinforc.tldr: DeepVideo-R1 improves video reasoning by combining an advantage-regression version of GRPO with difficulty-aware prompt and video augmentation.

paragraphs: Linear attention offers a computationally efficient approximation to softmax attention, making it attractive for long sequences. When converting a pretrained transformer to linear attention, an important choice is the feature dimension used for the approximation. Giving every layer the same dimension overlooks differences in what those layers need to represent.

The paper chooses feature dimensions automatically using statistical degrees of freedom, a measure of effective input dimensionality. The authors derive a bound on approximation error and show that their dimension selection achieves smaller errors under a fixed computational budget. They also introduce layerwise training to learn nonlinear features suited to each layer.

Experiments across multiple pretrained transformers show improved performance over baseline distillation methods without increasing inference cost. The central benefit is a better allocation of representational capacity across layers, combined with features adapted to those layers. The findings also reveal how attention complexity varies through a transformer, providing information about its internal structure as well as a method for making its attention more efficient.
neurips-2025-degrees-of-freedom-for-line.tldr: The method uses statistical degrees of freedom to allocate linear-attention feature dimensions across layers, improving distilled models without increasing inference cost.

paragraphs: Language models can still produce unsatisfactory responses after reinforcement learning from human feedback. This paper investigates a targeted repair strategy: identify training examples associated with an unwanted response, then unlearn those examples. It connects an explanation of a particular failure with an intervention intended to improve the model's behavior.

The explanation stage searches for training examples close to the problematic prompt-response pair in a feature representation. It imposes an additional requirement: the pair must be expressible as a convex combination of the selected examples in that space, meaning a weighted mixture with nonnegative weights summing to one. An iterative selection algorithm addresses this constrained optimization problem.

The second stage unlearns the identified data. The authors report improvement on unsatisfactory responses to some prompts without significantly degrading satisfactory responses to others, and their experiments demonstrate that the algorithm can improve RLHF. The result supports targeted data-based repair in the evaluated setting, with the feature-space explanation supplying the examples on which that repair operates.
neurips-2025-explainable-reinforcement-l.tldr: The paper links unwanted RLHF responses to selected training examples and unlearns those examples to improve some responses while largely preserving satisfactory behavior.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation adjusts a model when deployment data differ from its training data. FIND targets the harder situation where a single batch contains examples from multiple changing distributions. The authors observe that features from different domains form groups with different means and variances, making global normalization distort the original feature characteristics.

FIND first builds graph structures at individual layers to identify features with similar distributions. Its feature-aware batch normalization then combines source statistics with statistics specific to the test-time distributions. Together, these steps allow normalization to reflect groups within a batch instead of treating the whole batch as one homogeneous population.

A selective component decides which layers need this partitioning and which can remain unified, improving inference efficiency. Experiments report gains of up to approximately 30% in accuracy in dynamic scenarios while maintaining computational efficiency. The stated maximum is an observed result, and the broader contribution is an adaptation framework that explicitly handles distribution differences within the same incoming batch.
neurips-2025-feature-based-instance-neig.tldr: FIND adapts normalization to distribution-specific feature groups within test batches, reporting accuracy improvements of up to approximately 30% in dynamic scenarios.

paragraphs: VIPGuard studies personalized deepfake detection for a known person whose authentic facial data are available. That prior knowledge provides a way to examine whether a suspicious face matches the person's detailed characteristics. The framework aims to make both an accurate detection decision and an understandable explanation of that decision.

Its training proceeds through three stages. A multimodal language model first learns detailed facial attributes and structure. Identity-level discriminative learning then teaches it to distinguish subtle differences among similar faces, including real and fake versions. Finally, user-specific customization models the target person's characteristics and supports semantic reasoning over facial comparisons.

The authors also introduce VIPBench, an identity-aware benchmark incorporating seven face-swapping techniques and seven techniques for synthesizing entire faces. Their experiments show improvements over existing methods in detection and explanation. The approach makes known identity information central to the task: detailed knowledge of a particular face informs the comparison and provides material for explaining why a face appears authentic or manipulated.
neurips-2025-guard-me-if-you-know-me-pro.tldr: VIPGuard uses detailed knowledge of a known person's face to improve personalized deepfake detection and generate understandable explanations.

paragraphs: HumanCrafter addresses two tasks from a single image: reconstructing a three-dimensional human and assigning semantic labels to human parts. High visual fidelity alone does not provide the part-level understanding needed for segmentation. The paper therefore develops a unified, feed-forward framework that models appearance and human-part semantics together.

The reconstruction stage incorporates prior knowledge about human geometry, while the segmentation stage uses self-supervised semantic priors. Pixel-aligned aggregation connects information across the two tasks. A shared multi-task objective simultaneously encourages faithful texture modeling and consistent semantic labels, making the connection between reconstruction and segmentation part of the training process.

Because labeled 3D human data are scarce, the authors also develop an interactive annotation procedure to create high-quality data-label pairs. Experiments show that HumanCrafter exceeds existing state-of-the-art methods on both single-image human reconstruction and 3D human-part segmentation. These findings support joint modeling as a way to improve both visual reconstruction and the part-level interpretation of the resulting human representation.
neurips-2025-humancrafter-synergizing-ge.tldr: HumanCrafter jointly reconstructs a 3D human and labels body parts from one image, improving both tasks through shared geometric and semantic information.

paragraphs: Long-context modeling requires retaining dependencies across extended sequences. This paper develops a theoretical framework based on bipartite mutual information, which measures shared information between two portions of a sequence. The authors rigorously verify a scaling law for this quantity in natural language and use it to study the information a model must preserve.

A key finding is that bipartite mutual information captures interactions involving multiple tokens that are distinct from conventional two-point dependencies. These interactions also scale independently of two-point mutual information. Accounting for them provides a fuller description of the dependencies relevant to accurately modeling long sequences.

The resulting L²M condition places a lower bound on how a model's history state must scale for effective long-context modeling. This state consists of latent variables that store past information, so the condition expresses a necessary capacity requirement. The authors validate the framework and its predictions on transformers and state-space models. It offers a basis for architecture design, with applications beyond natural language presented as a possibility.
neurips-2025-l-2-m-mutual-information-sc.tldr: L²M uses a mutual-information scaling law to derive a necessary lower bound on the history-state capacity required for effective long-context modeling.

paragraphs: Models that predict neuronal activity from visual input and behavior can assign each neuron a learned representation. Such representations could help organize neurons by function or identify cell types. However, strong predictive models of mouse V1 do not naturally produce clearly separated groups, raising a question about whether the cause lies in the models or the biology.

DECEMber adds an explicit preference for clustered representations during model training. An auxiliary loss inspired by the t-distribution encourages structure among neuron embeddings. The method jointly learns those embeddings and the clustering parameters, using expectation maximization to update cluster centers and scale matrices.

The authors report more consistent clusters and greater stability than standard clustering methods while retaining high predictive performance. They also demonstrate generalization across mice and primates and across retina, V1, and V4. These findings show that a clustering preference can produce stable organization without sacrificing the prediction task. Because the method deliberately encourages clusters, its stated contribution is improved representation and clustering behavior rather than a resolution of the original biological question.
neurips-2025-learning-to-cluster-neurona.tldr: DECEMber explicitly encourages neuronal embeddings to form stable clusters while preserving high activity-prediction performance across tested species and visual areas.

paragraphs: A policy learned in one environment may be deployed where actions lead to different state transitions. Distributionally robust decision processes address this by optimizing performance against the worst environment in a specified uncertainty set. This paper studies how to construct that set when prior knowledge describes the dynamics as a linear mixture.

The proposed framework assumes that nominal transition dynamics follow a linear mixture model. It places uncertainty around the mixture weights, rather than directly around the full transition kernel. The authors show that this gives a more refined representation of uncertainty than conventional rectangular uncertainty models when relevant knowledge of the mixture structure is available.

They also develop a general robust-policy learning algorithm for uncertainty sets defined through f-divergences. Sample-complexity analyses cover total variation, Kullback-Leibler, and chi-squared divergences. These results establish statistical learnability for the new setting. The main contribution is a theoretical framework whose uncertainty model makes explicit use of known structure in the transition dynamics.
neurips-2025-linear-mixture-distribution.tldr: The paper models transition uncertainty through linear-mixture weights and establishes robust-policy learning guarantees for several divergence-based uncertainty sets.

paragraphs: Multimodal learning combines information from different types of input. MANGO addresses the difficulty of representing both the essential features of each modality and the complex relationships between them. The paper argues that standard attention-based fusion learns these correlations implicitly, motivating a framework designed to make fusion explicit, interpretable, and mathematically tractable.

The core component is an invertible cross-attention layer within a normalizing-flow model. The authors introduce three mechanisms for modeling cross-modal relationships: Modality-to-Modality Cross-Attention, Inter-Modality Cross-Attention, and Learnable Inter-Modality Cross-Attention. These mechanisms are incorporated into a multimodal flow architecture intended to scale to high-dimensional inputs.

The approach is evaluated on semantic segmentation, image-to-image translation, and movie genre classification, with state-of-the-art performance reported across these three tasks. The contribution combines an architectural requirement—invertible attention—with explicit modeling of multimodal correlations. Its results indicate that this structured fusion approach can support strong predictive performance across several different kinds of multimodal learning problems.
neurips-2025-mango-multimodal-attention-.tldr: MANGO combines invertible cross-attention with normalizing flows for explicit multimodal fusion, reporting state-of-the-art results on three tasks.

paragraphs: Formal theorem proving requires selecting logically valid steps within a vast search space. Language-model-based stepwise provers can guide this process, but biased guidance can repeatedly favor unproductive routes. MPS-Prover addresses both the training data used to guide proof construction and the search procedure that chooses which tactics to explore.

Its data-curation strategy removes approximately 40% of redundant post-training data without sacrificing performance. Its multi-perspective tree search combines a learned critic with deliberately designed heuristic rules. These different sources of guidance diversify tactic selection, help avoid unproductive states, and improve the robustness of the search.

Evaluations report state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmarks including miniF2F and ProofNet, exceeding prior models with seven billion parameters. Further analysis finds significantly shorter and more diverse proofs than existing stepwise and whole-proof methods. The findings connect improved proof success with the structure of the proofs produced: the system explores more varied strategies while arriving at more compact solutions in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2025-mps-prover-advancing-stepwi.tldr: MPS-Prover combines substantial training-data pruning with critic-and-heuristic search to produce stronger benchmark results and shorter, more diverse proofs.

paragraphs: This paper studies a trading platform that repeatedly sets a unit price for a new supplier and retailer. The supplier has a private production cost, and the retailer has a private utility function. The platform must learn how to price trades from the decisions these participants communicate, while aiming to maximize social welfare.

At each interaction, the supplier accepts or rejects the proposed price, while the retailer independently chooses a purchase quantity at that price. Trade occurs only if the supplier accepts. The retailer then buys its chosen quantity and pays the supplier the quantity multiplied by the unit price. This makes pricing depend on both willingness to supply and quantity demanded.

The authors design an online pricing strategy with sharp regret rates under specified natural assumptions. They also examine those assumptions and prove that relaxing any of them makes the problem unlearnable in their setting. The contribution therefore includes both a successful learning strategy and a characterization of conditions necessary for the stated learnability result.
neurips-2025-online-learning-in-the-repe.tldr: The paper derives sharp regret guarantees for repeated mediated pricing under assumptions whose relaxation makes the studied problem unlearnable.

paragraphs: Recognizing social interaction requires attention to small signals such as gaze, facial expression, and gestures. The paper argues that representing each person only as a whole can obscure those signals. It also identifies ambiguity in predicting groups directly without first modeling the interactions that connect their members.

The proposed framework builds groups from individuals and their relationships. It first detects people and enriches their representations with body-part features. Similarity-based reasoning then associates individuals into groups, considering spatial relationships together with the subtle social cues carried by those features. Group configuration is therefore inferred through evidence of interpersonal interaction.

Experiments on the NVI dataset show performance above prior methods, establishing a new state of the art on that dataset. The approach matters because group membership depends on more than where people stand: localized visual signals contribute evidence about how they relate. The reported results support combining part-level information with bottom-up group reasoning for fine-grained social interaction detection.
neurips-2025-part-aware-bottom-up-group-.tldr: The framework uses body-part cues and interpersonal relationships to infer social groups, achieving state-of-the-art results on NVI.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can lose performance when their training or fine-tuning data are imbalanced. Some image-text pairs represent majority data, while others belong to much less represented minority data. PoGDiff addresses this imbalance through a general fine-tuning approach that changes the target distribution used during learning.

The usual objective compares a predicted distribution with a ground-truth distribution through KL divergence. PoGDiff replaces that ground-truth target with a Product of Gaussians. This revised target combines the original ground-truth information with a predicted distribution conditioned on a neighboring text embedding, incorporating information associated with nearby text representations into the learning target.

Experiments on real-world datasets show improvements in both generation accuracy and image quality, supporting the method's effectiveness against the studied imbalance problem. The central idea is to change how supervision is constructed: each target incorporates both its original information and a prediction connected to neighboring text. The reported findings establish an empirical benefit for this fine-tuning strategy in imbalanced text-to-image generation.
neurips-2025-pogdiff-product-of-gaussian.tldr: PoGDiff improves generation on imbalanced datasets by fine-tuning diffusion models against targets that combine ground truth with predictions from neighboring text embeddings.

paragraphs: Training multimodal models for segmentation often depends on manually prepared data that include explicit reasoning processes. Producing such annotations is costly and time-consuming. SAM-R1 explores reinforcement learning as a way to develop fine-grained image understanding and segmentation-oriented reasoning without depending on that form of reasoning annotation.

The framework incorporates fine-grained segmentation into multimodal reasoning training. It combines task-specific rewards with an optimization objective designed to align reasoning and segmentation. The Segment Anything Model, or SAM, acts as a flexible reward provider, supplying feedback that guides the learning process toward the segmentation task.

Using only 3,000 training samples, SAM-R1 achieves strong performance across multiple benchmarks. The reported result supports the effectiveness of reinforcement learning for teaching segmentation-oriented reasoning with a relatively small training set. Its main contribution is the connection between a segmentation model that provides rewards and a multimodal model learning to reason: the feedback is tied directly to the fine-grained visual task the model is intended to perform.
neurips-2025-sam-r1-leveraging-sam-for-r.tldr: SAM-R1 uses SAM-provided rewards to train segmentation-oriented multimodal reasoning, achieving strong benchmark performance with 3,000 training samples.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning depends on choosing examples relevant to the task a model should improve at. This paper argues that common text representations may miss how the particular model internally processes those examples. It therefore represents samples through the model's own activation patterns when deciding which training data match a target task.

Raw activations create a complication: one neuron can respond to multiple unrelated concepts, making unrelated samples appear similar. The method uses sparse autoencoders to separate these mixed responses into sparse, monosemantic representations. It then applies a similarity measure designed specifically for that representation space to identify task-relevant examples.

Experiments cover multiple instruction datasets, models, tasks, and proportions of selected data. Across those evaluations, the method consistently exceeds existing selection baselines in stability and task-specific performance. The findings support using a model's internal computation to guide data selection, provided that mixed neuron responses are disentangled before measuring similarity. The contribution joins representation design and sample comparison within a single selection strategy.
neurips-2025-task-specific-data-selectio.tldr: The method selects instruction-tuning examples using sparse, disentangled model activations, improving selection stability and target-task performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Synthetic time series need to remain useful while allowing their source to be verified. TimeWak addresses watermarking for multivariate diffusion generators that operate directly in data space. Existing watermarking approaches designed for homogeneous latent spaces do not fit this setting, where features differ and measurements depend on their position in time.

TimeWak embeds a temporal chained-hashing watermark directly across the temporal-feature data space. For detection, its epsilon-exact inversion addresses reconstruction errors that are distributed unevenly across features when reversing the diffusion process. The authors also derive an inversion error bound while preserving robust watermark detectability.

Evaluations span five datasets, different temporal lengths, and post-editing attacks, examining data quality, detectability, and robustness. Against the strongest baseline, TimeWak reports improvements of 61.96% in context-FID and 8.44% in correlational scores while remaining consistently detectable. These findings support a watermarking design that accounts for temporal structure and feature differences while preserving the usefulness of the generated data.
neurips-2025-timewak-temporal-chained-ha.tldr: TimeWak watermarks multivariate diffusion-generated time series directly in data space, improving reported quality metrics while maintaining watermark detectability.

paragraphs: In high-dimensional linear regression, a model can fit its training data exactly and still generalize well, a phenomenon called benign overfitting. This paper studies how transfer learning interacts with the minimum-L2-norm interpolator, which selects an exact-fitting solution with minimum coefficient norm. It asks when data from other sources improve the target task.

The authors propose a two-step Transfer MNI method and characterize its finite-sample excess risk. Their analysis identifies conditions under which it improves on an interpolator trained only on target data. It also identifies covariate-shift regimes where heterogeneous source data provide transfer benefits at limited cost, described as free-lunch regimes.

To make these results operational, the paper introduces a data-driven procedure for identifying informative sources and an ensemble that combines multiple informative Transfer MNIs. Finite-sample experiments show robustness to model and data heterogeneity and confirm an advantage for the proposed methods. The contribution combines conditional theoretical guarantees with mechanisms for selecting and combining useful sources.
neurips-2025-transfer-learning-for-benig.tldr: Transfer MNI identifies conditions where heterogeneous source data improve benign overfitting and provides procedures to select and combine informative sources.

paragraphs: Optimization-based text-to-3D methods often obtain guidance from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models through Score Distillation Sampling, or SDS. That process can introduce oversaturated colors and excessive smoothing. This paper instead frames generation around a direct transport trajectory between the current rendering distribution and the desired target distribution.

The authors establish a theoretical connection between SDS and the Schrödinger Bridge framework. Under specific conditions, such as having Gaussian noise at one endpoint, the bridge's reverse process reduces to the score function used by SDS. This conditional connection motivates Trajectory-Centric Distillation, or TraCe.

TraCe explicitly constructs a diffusion bridge from the current rendering to its text-conditioned, denoised target. It trains a LoRA-adapted model on the trajectory's score dynamics to guide 3D optimization. The framework enables high-quality generation with smaller classifier-free guidance values, and experiments report consistently better quality and fidelity than state-of-the-art techniques. Its central change is to make the path from current rendering to target explicit in the guidance process.
neurips-2025-walking-the-schrodinger-bri.tldr: TraCe uses a Schrödinger Bridge-inspired trajectory from current renderings to text-conditioned targets to improve text-to-3D quality with smaller guidance values.

paragraphs: Invisible watermarks are intended to support image provenance, but forged marks can falsely attribute content to a provider. WMCopier investigates this failure mode by introducing an attack that does not require prior knowledge of or access to the target watermarking algorithm. The work tests whether a detected mark remains trustworthy under forgery.

At a high level, the approach uses an unconditional diffusion model to represent the target watermark distribution. A shallow inversion process then embeds the target watermark into an initially unwatermarked image. An iterative refinement procedure adjusts the reconstruction to trade off image fidelity against forgery efficiency.

Experiments show that WMCopier deceives both open-source and closed-source watermark systems, including Amazon's system, with substantially higher success than existing methods. The authors also evaluate the robustness of forged images and discuss a possible defense. The findings expose a provenance problem: successful watermark detection can support false attribution when the mark itself has been forged, making forgery resistance an important property to evaluate.
neurips-2025-wmcopier-forging-invisible-.tldr: WMCopier demonstrates watermark forgery without access to the target algorithm, achieving higher reported attack success against open- and closed-source systems.
